897.title: Josephine Bakhita (c. 1869–1947)
897.hook: kidnapped in Sudan, enslaved, freed, she became a sister, patron of trafficking survivors
897.howItsDone: Catholics keep Josephine Bakhita's feast in February, and many parishes and religious orders use the day to pray for victims and survivors of human trafficking and to support groups that help them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Uganda martyrs, among them Charles Lwanga, young men who died for Christ under one king. Your line was catholic and anglican together. Did you pray for Uganda? Today, a woman who once had no name she could remember. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

A girl in Sudan is grabbed by slave raiders. She is so terrified that, by her own later telling, she forgets the name her parents gave her. The raiders hand her another name: Bakhita. She is sold, and sold again. Owners beat her. One has her skin cut in patterns and rubbed with salt, so the scars will stay. Then an Italian consul buys her, and she ends up in Italy, caring for a family's little daughter. The family leaves the two of them for a while with some sisters in Venice. Something happens in that convent that ends with the law in Venice deciding who she belongs to.
screen: `A GIRL TAKEN BY RAIDERS.` → `SOLD, AND SOLD AGAIN.` → `A CONVENT IN VENICE.`

segments.voice: Begin with what she kept. First, the scars. Bakhita carried them on her body for the rest of her life. She never pretended the cruelty hadn't happened. Second, the convent. The Canossian Sisters in Venice taught her about God, and about Christ, who also suffered at the hands of others. She asked to be baptized. Third, the refusal. When her mistress came back to take her home, Bakhita said no. She wanted to stay. The mistress pushed, and the case went to the authorities in Venice. They ruled that she was free: under Italian law, nobody could own her. So she was freed by a legal ruling. Fourth, the deeper freedom. She was baptized with the name Josephine, and kept Bakhita too. Later she joined the Canossian Sisters herself, and for years she cooked, sewed, and answered the convent door in a small town. People came to the door just to talk to her. Pope Benedict XVI told her story in his letter on hope. He wrote that after cruel masters, she came to know a different master, one who loved her, and that this gave her hope. In the Gospel of John, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "If therefore the son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed." Freed by a ruling. Free, she said, by being loved. The Church now names her as a patron of people who survive trafficking, the slavery that still goes on.
screen: `THE SCARS SHE CARRIED.` · `BAPTISM ASKED FOR.` · `SHE SAID NO.` · `FREE BY BEING LOVED.` · then, large: `FREE INDEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for trafficking survivors. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind the people, right now, who are bought and sold, or who have just gotten out. A worker who can't leave a job. A girl far from home. Someone rebuilding a life. You don't need faces; let them be real anyway. If you pray, you can ask Josephine Bakhita to stand with them, or just hold them before God in silence. If you don't pray, hold them in your attention and wish them freedom. The bell holds the time.
Josephine Bakhita. A woman enslaved as a girl, declared free in Venice, baptized, and made a sister, now a patron of trafficking survivors.
Your line: freed and free. Today, look at one thing you buy, a shirt or a bag of coffee, and ask who made it, and whether they could walk away. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

898.title: Katharine Drexel (1858–1955)
898.hook: an heiress who gave her fortune to schools for Black and Native Americans
898.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States keep Katharine Drexel's feast in March; the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament, Xavier University of Louisiana and Black and Native American Catholic communities mark it with Mass and service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Josephine Bakhita, declared free by a court in Venice and free, she said, by being loved. Your line was freed and free. Did you ask who made something you bought? Today, a banker's daughter and a question from a pope. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

Rome, and a young woman from a banking family in Philadelphia is kneeling before Pope Leo XIII. She has come to ask a favor. Back home she has seen missions among Native American peoples that are short of priests, and she wants the Pope to send missionaries. Tradition says he looked at her and answered with a question of his own: why not become a missionary yourself? It was not the answer she came for. That question changed the plan. Her name is Katharine Drexel.
screen: `A BANKER'S DAUGHTER IN ROME.` → `SEND MISSIONARIES, PLEASE.` → `WHY NOT YOU?`

segments.voice: The money comes first, so start there. First, the inheritance. Her father, Francis Drexel, was a wealthy banker, and when he died, the income from his fortune passed to his daughters. Katharine's share was large. Second, the vow. Instead of marrying or living quietly with the money, she became a sister and founded a new community, the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament. Their work was with Native Americans and Black Americans, among them children whom segregated schools often turned away. Third, the giving. Year after year she paid for schools, missions and churches, in the West and the South, in cities and on reservations. In New Orleans she and her sisters founded what became Xavier University of Louisiana. People wrote to her asking for help, and she answered letter after letter. She spent the money on others, and her biographers say she lived plainly herself: worn shoes, patched clothes, pencils used down to the stub. Fourth, the quiet end. After illness she spent her last years mostly in prayer, in a small room near the chapel, close to the Blessed Sacrament she had named her sisters for. In the Gospel of Matthew, a rich young man asks Jesus what he must do, and Jesus tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow. The young man walks away sad, because he has many possessions. Katharine Drexel heard the same Gospel and did not walk away. She gave the fortune. The Church has since canonized her.
screen: `A BANKER'S FORTUNE.` · `THE SISTERS OF THE BLESSED SACRAMENT.` · `SCHOOLS PAID FOR, YEAR AFTER YEAR.` · `A QUIET ROOM BY THE CHAPEL.` · then, large: `SHE DID NOT WALK AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give to an education cause. Settle first, and breathe. Let a child or a student come to mind, someone whose chance to learn is fragile. A school near you, a scholarship fund, a library, a tutoring program. Hold one of them in your mind. If you pray, you can pray for the students there by name or by face. If you don't, simply stay with them. When the bell rings, decide on one gift, any size, money or time or a box of books. The bell holds the time.
Katharine Drexel. A Philadelphia heiress who became a sister and spent her inheritance on schools for Black and Native Americans.
Your line: she gave the fortune. Today, make that one gift to someone's learning, however small: money, an hour, or a book. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

899.title: Frances Cabrini (1850–1917)
899.hook: an Italian sister who served immigrants in America, patron of immigrants
899.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States keep Frances Cabrini's feast in November; parishes and Catholic charities often mark it with prayer for migrants and with service to immigrant families, and pilgrims visit her shrines in New York, Chicago and Colorado.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Katharine Drexel, who heard the Pope ask why not you, and spent her inheritance on schools. Your line was she gave the fortune. Did a small gift go somewhere? Today, a sister who wanted to go east and was sent west. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

New York harbor, and a ship from Italy is coming in. On deck stands a small woman in a religious habit, with a few sisters beside her. She was not supposed to be here at all. Since childhood she had dreamed of being a missionary in China, and she founded her own community of sisters with that in mind. Then, in Rome, she was sent the other way. And, tradition says, she is afraid of water. Her name is Frances Xavier Cabrini.
screen: `A SHIP INTO NEW YORK.` → `A DREAM OF CHINA.` → `SENT THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Start with the order she was given. First, the redirect. Her community was the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart, and she went to Rome to ask permission to take them to China. Tradition says Pope Leo XIII told her: not to the East, but to the West. Italian families were arriving in American cities, often poor, with few priests or sisters who spoke their language. Second, the arrival. When she and her sisters landed, tradition says the house they'd been promised wasn't ready, and the archbishop suggested they might go back to Italy. She stayed. Third, the work and the crossings. She and her sisters ran classes for immigrant children, opened orphanages, and started hospitals, beginning in New York and spreading to other cities and countries. Her sisters went into tenements and jails, wherever Italian families were struggling. She was afraid of water; tradition says she had nearly drowned as a child. Yet she crossed the ocean again and again, because the work kept calling her back and forth. Fourth, the citizen. She became an American citizen herself. She died in Chicago, and the Church later canonized her and named her a patron of immigrants. Catholics hear the words of Jesus about the final judgment in the Gospel of Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." For Cabrini, the stranger was the family off the boat, the child in a crowded room, the sick person far from home. That's why people call her the immigrants' saint: she spent her life on immigrants, and became one herself.
screen: `NOT EAST, BUT WEST.` · `A HOUSE THAT WASN'T READY.` · `SCHOOLS, HOSPITALS, CROSSINGS.` · `AN IMMIGRANT HERSELF.` · then, large: `I WAS A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help an immigrant. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who came from somewhere else. A neighbor, a coworker, a person who cleans your building, maybe someone in your own family tree. Think about what the first weeks might have been like: the forms, the language, the not knowing where anything is. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, hold them in your attention. When the bell rings, pick one concrete help: a ride, a translation, a meal, a patient conversation. The bell holds the time.
Frances Cabrini. An Italian sister sent west instead of east, who built schools and hospitals for immigrants and became one herself.
Your line: the immigrants' saint. Today, learn one thing about where a neighbor or coworker came from, by asking and then listening. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

900.title: Story of a Soul (1898)
900.hook: Thérèse's memoir is published and goes around the world
900.howItsDone: Some Catholics read Story of a Soul on retreat or around Thérèse's feast in October, and parishes and prayer groups sometimes read it together a chapter at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Frances Cabrini, sent west instead of east, an immigrant serving immigrants. Your line was the immigrants' saint. Did you ask someone where they came from? Today, a book nobody planned to sell. Day nine hundred.

A notebook, a pen, and a young nun in a Carmelite convent in Lisieux, in France. Her older sister, who is also her prioress, has asked her to write down memories of their childhood. So Thérèse writes: her family, her mother's death, her tears, her first communion, the convent. Later, already sick, she is asked to write more, and she keeps going in a garden chair, then in bed. She did not begin it as a book for strangers; only near the end does she speak of the pages being printed. After she dies, the convent prints them. Today: Story of a Soul.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK IN LISIEUX.` → `WRITTEN FOR HER SISTERS.` → `PRINTED AFTER SHE DIES.`

segments.voice: Follow the book in four steps. First, the writing. Thérèse wrote in pieces, under obedience, in ordinary notebooks. She wasn't composing a classic. She was answering her sisters. Second, the editing. Her sister Pauline, Mother Agnes, prepared the pages for print and smoothed them in places. Much later, the original notebooks were published as Thérèse wrote them, so readers could see her own words. Third, the spreading. Carmelite convents would send a short account of a sister's life to other houses after her death. This account was different. It was copied, reprinted, translated, passed from hand to hand. Tradition says letters came back to Lisieux from people who had read it: soldiers, mothers, missionaries, people in prison. Fourth, the little way. What readers found was not a story of great deeds. It was a way: do small things with love, trust God like a child, and don't wait to become impressive first. Catholics hear Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." Thérèse took that line seriously. The Church later canonized her and named her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Church. Much of what she taught reached readers through one little book, written for her sisters.
screen: `NOTEBOOKS, UNDER OBEDIENCE.` · `A SISTER'S EDITING.` · `PASSED HAND TO HAND.` · `THE LITTLE WAY.` · then, large: `BECOME AS LITTLE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one page of her story. If you have the book, open it anywhere and read a page slowly. If you don't, take the line from today: become as little children. Settle, and breathe. Let one small task from today come to mind: a dish, a message, a chore you've been avoiding. Go through it in your mind, slowly, done with care. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, simply notice how small and how real it is. The bell holds the time.

Little way. Thérèse's idea that small things done with love, and trusting God like a child, matter more than impressive deeds, the heart of the notebooks she wrote for her sisters, later printed as Story of a Soul.
Your line: a little book. Today, write down one memory for someone in your family, a page at most, and give it to them. Day nine hundred.

901.title: Communion for children (1905–1910)
901.hook: Pius X encourages frequent communion and first communion around age seven
901.howItsDone: In the Latin Church, Catholic children usually prepare for first communion at around seven or eight, often in a parish class, after a first confession; adults who are in a state of grace may receive communion at any Mass, even daily.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Story of a Soul, Thérèse's notebooks on the little way, written for her sisters, that traveled the world. Your line was a little book. Did you write a memory down for someone? Today, a pope who opened the altar rail to children. Day nine hundred one.

A white dress, or a small suit and tie. A row of children walking up the aisle, hands folded, trying not to giggle. Grandparents with cameras in the pews. In a Catholic parish, first communion is a big day, and it comes when a child is still small. That timing has a history. Before it changed, children were often kept waiting longer, and adults who did go to communion might go only rarely, out of a sense that they were never worthy enough. A pope named Pius X set out to change both habits.
screen: `A ROW OF CHILDREN IN THE AISLE.` → `A DAY THAT USED TO COME LATER.` → `A POPE CHANGES THE HABIT.`

segments.voice: Two documents did the work, and they answer one worry. First, the hesitation. A strict mood in parts of the Church had taught people to keep their distance from the altar, as if communion were a prize for the nearly perfect. Second, the invitation to adults. A decree under Pius X said that communion could be received often, even daily, by anyone in a state of grace who comes with a right intention. Communion was described not as a reward for the holy but as help for the weak. Come often. Third, the children. A second decree, known by its opening Latin words, Quam singulari, took up the age of first communion. It said the age of discretion is when a child begins to reason, about the seventh year, more or less, and that children should not be kept waiting long past it. A child didn't need to understand everything a theologian knows. They needed to know, in their own way, that this bread is not ordinary bread, and to want it. Fourth, the root. The decrees leaned on the words of Jesus in the Gospel of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "Except you eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you." If the bread is life, the reasoning went, why make the hungry wait? The small children walking up the aisle today follow a path opened by two documents from one pope.
screen: `KEEPING A DISTANCE.` · `HELP FOR THE WEAK, NOT A PRIZE.` · `THE AGE OF DISCRETION.` · `BREAD THAT IS LIFE.` · then, large: `COME OFTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your first communion. Settle, and breathe. If you made one, let the day come back: the clothes, the church, who was there, what you were thinking about. If you didn't, remember a first time at any table that mattered, a meal where you were welcomed. Notice who brought you there. If you pray, you can thank God for that person by name. If you don't, simply hold them in your thoughts with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Quam singulari. The decree under Pius X that said children should make their first communion once they reach the age of discretion, about seven years old.
Your line: come often. Today, go back to one good thing you've been keeping at a distance until you feel ready for it. Day nine hundred one.

902.title: Charles de Foucauld (1858–1916)
902.hook: a soldier turned hermit among the Tuareg, the universal brother, canonized a saint
902.howItsDone: Catholics keep Charles de Foucauld's memory on 1 December; communities inspired by him, such as the Little Brothers and Little Sisters of Jesus, live simply in small groups among poor neighbors and keep long times of silent prayer before the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, communion for children under Quam singulari, and a pope who called communion help for the weak. Your line was come often. Did you go back to something you'd kept at a distance? Today, a man who went a very long way to be a neighbor. Day nine hundred two.

A young French cavalry officer, rich, bored, and famous among his friends for parties and expensive food. He has lost his faith and doesn't miss it. He leaves the army, then travels through Morocco in disguise to map it, and the trip makes his name as an explorer. But something else follows him home: the memory of Muslims stopping to pray, again and again, every day. Back in Paris, he starts slipping into churches and repeating a strange little prayer: if you exist, let me know you. His name is Charles de Foucauld.
screen: `AN OFFICER WHO LOVES PARTIES.` → `MOROCCO, IN DISGUISE.` → `IF YOU EXIST, LET ME KNOW YOU.`

segments.voice: His life came in four stages. First, the confession. In a Paris church, he went to a priest, Abbé Huvelin, to talk about faith. The priest told him to kneel and confess, then sent him to communion. Charles later wrote that as soon as he believed there was a God, he knew he could only live for him. Second, Nazareth. He tried the strict life of a Trappist monastery, then left for Nazareth, where he worked as a handyman for a convent of sisters. He wanted to live the hidden years of Jesus, the carpenter's years nobody wrote down. Third, the desert. Ordained a priest, he went to the Sahara in French Algeria. At Beni Abbès he called his little house the fraternity. He settled at last at Tamanrasset, among the Tuareg people. He didn't preach sermons at them. He visited, nursed, shared tea, and spent years writing a Tuareg dictionary and collecting their poems. He wanted to be the universal brother, brother to Christians, Muslims, and anyone who knocked. Fourth, the door. During the upheavals of the war, raiders came to his house, and he was killed at his own door. He died alone, with no followers. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his followers: "one is your master; and all you are brethren." Charles took the second half as literally as the first. Groups of priests, sisters and laypeople now follow his way, and the Church has canonized him.
screen: `A PRIEST SAYS: KNEEL.` · `A HANDYMAN IN NAZARETH.` · `A DICTIONARY IN THE DESERT.` · `KILLED AT HIS DOOR.` · then, large: `ALL YOU ARE BRETHREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a brother to someone. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who sits a little outside your circle. The one who eats lunch alone, a neighbor you've never spoken to, someone whose language or faith is different from yours. Don't plan a speech. Just hold them in your attention as a brother or a sister. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. When the bell rings, think of one small way to visit, the way Charles did: a cup of tea, a question, some time. The bell holds the time.
Universal brother. What Charles de Foucauld wanted to be among the Tuareg: brother to Christians, Muslims, and anyone who knocked at his door.
Your line: brother to everyone. Today, learn one word in someone else's language, and use it with them. Day nine hundred two.

903.title: Fatima, 1917
903.hook: three shepherd children and a call to prayer and penance
903.howItsDone: Catholics keep Our Lady of Fatima on 13 May; pilgrims go to the shrine at Fatima, and in parishes people pray the rosary together, often adding a prayer for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles de Foucauld, the soldier who became the universal brother to the Tuareg. Your line was brother to everyone. Did you learn a word in someone else's language? Today, shepherd children, and a jail cell. Day nine hundred three.

A town official in Portugal loads some children into his carriage. They are shepherds from the hamlet of Aljustrel, near Fatima: Lucia and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta. For months they have said that a lady from heaven appears to them on the thirteenth of each month, and crowds now follow them to the field. The official is not a believer, and his government is suspicious of the Church. He wants the crowds gone and the children's secret out. Instead of taking them to the field, he takes them to his town and locks them up.
screen: `A CARRIAGE, A TOWN OFFICIAL.` → `CROWDS IN A FIELD.` → `CHILDREN LOCKED UP.`

segments.voice: Stay with those few days, from the field to the cell. First, the message. The children said the lady asked them to pray the rosary every day for peace and for the end of the war, and to do penance, small sacrifices offered for others. Europe was at war, and Portuguese soldiers were in it. Second, the pressure. In Lucia's later memoirs, the official questioned them, and when they refused to tell what the lady had confided to them, he threatened them with death. They were frightened. They still wouldn't tell. Third, the cell. Lucia recalled that the children were put in a room with the town's prisoners. Jacinta was crying for her mother. Then the children knelt and began to pray the rosary, and some of the prisoners knelt and prayed with them. Grown men in a jail, following children through the Hail Mary. Fourth, the outcome. The children were sent home, and they said the lady came to them again a few days later, in a different spot. In the end the Church judged the appearances worthy of belief; Catholics are free to accept or not, since the Church calls such events private revelations. At its center is a prayer older than Fatima: the angel's words in the Gospel of Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." This week ran through a freed slave, an heiress, an immigrant, a little book, children at the altar, a desert brother, and now children praying in a jail.
